hand/geometric-langlands.html:
Categorical Langlands Correspondence and Derived Operators

The geometric Langlands program lifts the classical correspondence of representations to an equivalence of categories. On the automorphic side one works with the derived category of D‑modules on the moduli stack BunG of G‑bundles on a smooth projective curve X. On the spectral side the object is the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the stack LocL G(X) of L G‑local systems. The equivalence is expected to intertwine the action of Hecke operators — which modify a bundle at a point — with the operation of tensoring by the corresponding representation of the dual group. In the categorical formulation the Hecke functors become exact endofunctors of D‑mod(BunG) and the eigensheaf condition is replaced by the requirement that an object be an eigenobject for all Hecke functors simultaneously. This leads to the notion of a Hecke eigensheaf in the derived sense: a complex of D‑modules equipped with isomorphisms to its Hecke transforms that satisfy the appropriate compatibilities. The categorical equivalence also respects the monoidal structures given by convolution on the affine Grassmannian and by tensor product of local systems, making it a tensor equivalence of symmetric monoidal ∞‑categories.

Derived Hecke functors

For each dominant coweight λ of G one defines a Hecke correspondence Heckeλ ⊂ BunG × X × BunG. The associated functor Hλ sends a D‑module F to the push‑forward along the second projection of the pull‑back along the first projection, twisted by the determinant line bundle. In the derived setting these functors are exact and preserve the subcategory of holonomic D‑modules. The commutativity of Hecke functors for different λ follows from the factorization property of the affine Grassmannian, which is a geometric incarnation of the tensor category of representations of L G.

Eigenobjects and the spectral decomposition

An eigenobject E in D‑mod(BunG) with eigenvalue a local system 𝔼 on X is an object equipped with isomorphisms Hλ(E) ≅ Vλ ⊗ E, where Vλ is the representation of L G of highest weight λ. The collection of such isomorphisms for all λ assembles into a factorization structure that identifies the endomorphism algebra of E with the algebra of functions on the moduli of local systems. The categorical Langlands conjecture asserts that the functor sending a local system 𝔼 to its eigensheaf E𝔼 induces an equivalence of categories after suitable completions. This equivalence is compatible with the natural t‑structures and sends standard objects (Δ‑modules) to skyscraper sheaves on LocL G(X).

Affine Grassmannian and Geometric Satake Equivalence

The affine Grassmannian GrG = G(𝒦)/G(𝒪) — where 𝒦 = ℂ((t)) and 𝒪 = ℂ[[t]] — is an ind‑scheme whose ℂ‑points parametrize G‑bundles on the formal disc together with a trivialization on the punctured disc. Its geometry encodes the representation theory of the Langlands dual group L G. The geometric Satake equivalence, proved by Ginzburg, Mirković–Vilonen, and others, constructs a tensor equivalence between the category of G(𝒪)‑equivariant perverse sheaves on GrG (with convolution product) and the category Rep(L G) of finite‑dimensional representations of L G. Under this equivalence the intersection cohomology complex ICλ of the Schubert variety Grλ corresponds to the irreducible representation Vλ of highest weight λ.

Convolution and factorization

The convolution product on perverse sheaves is defined using the diagram GrG × GrG ← GrG ×G(𝒪) GrG → GrG. The factorization property states that for a curve X the global affine Grassmannian GrG,X over Xn satisfies a compatibility with the local affine Grassmannians at each point. This factorization is the geometric source of the commutativity of Hecke functors and of the braiding in the category of D‑modules on BunG. The geometric Satake equivalence is functorial with respect to homomorphisms of groups, and it intertwines the natural fiber functor on Rep(L G) with the global sections functor on perverse sheaves.

Applications to Hecke eigensheaves

Given a local system 𝔼 on X, the geometric Satake equivalence allows one to construct the Hecke eigensheaf E𝔼 as a colimit of convolution powers of the basic Hecke functors applied to the delta D‑module at the trivial bundle. The eigenvalue property follows from the identification of the convolution algebra with the representation ring of L G. In the categorical Langlands program the Satake equivalence is used to define the spectral action of Rep(L G) on D‑mod(BunG) and to prove that the resulting functor to QCoh(LocL G(X)) is fully faithful on a large subcategory.

Worked Example: Computing a Hecke Transform on the Affine Grassmannian
Let G = SL₂ and λ the fundamental coweight. Describe the Hecke correspondence Heckeλ and compute the effect of the Hecke functor Hλ on the delta D‑module δ1 supported at the trivial bundle on BunSL₂.
The affine Grassmannian GrSL₂ has Schubert cells indexed by non‑negative integers n. The fundamental coweight corresponds to n = 1, so Grλ is the closure of the cell of dimension 1, isomorphic to ℙ¹. The Hecke correspondence Heckeλ is the subvariety of Bun × X × Bun consisting of triples (ℰ, x, ℰ') where ℰ' is obtained from ℰ by an elementary modification of type λ at x. Over a fixed point x ∈ X the fiber is Grλ ≅ ℙ¹. The delta D‑module δ1 pulls back to the structure sheaf of the constant section. Pushing forward along the second projection integrates over the ℙ¹ fiber, producing the intersection cohomology complex ICλ on Grλ viewed as a D‑module on Bun. By geometric Satake, ICλ corresponds to the standard representation V of SL₂. Hence Hλ(δ1) is the D‑module on Bun whose fiber at a bundle ℰ is the space of sections of the associated rank‑2 vector bundle, i.e. the Hecke transform of the trivial bundle is the universal rank‑2 bundle on Bun × X.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the relationship between the affine Grassmannian and Hecke operators, recall that the convolution product on GrG categorifies the tensor product of representations of L G. State the geometric Satake equivalence explicitly and note that the Hecke functor Hλ is the convolution with ICλ. This connects the local geometry of GrG to the global Hecke action on BunG.

Critical Level, Feigin–Frenkel Center, and Opers

At the critical level k = −h∨ the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence simplifies dramatically because the center of the completed universal enveloping algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤̂ becomes large. Feigin and Frenkel proved that this center Zcrit(𝔤̂) is canonically isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of L G‑opers on the formal disc. An L G‑oper is a L G‑bundle with a connection and a reduction to a Borel subgroup satisfying a transversality condition; globally on X an oper is a L G‑local system with a compatible flag structure. The Feigin–Frenkel isomorphism identifies the action of Zcrit on any critical‑level representation with the evaluation of functions on the corresponding oper.

Opers and the classical limit

The space OpL G(X) of global opers is a finite‑dimensional algebraic variety that embeds into LocL G(X) as a Lagrangian subvariety with respect to the natural symplectic structure. In the classical limit ℏ → 0 the quantum Hitchin system reduces to the Hitchin integrable system, and the spectral curve of an oper coincides with the Hitchin spectral curve. The quantization parameter ℏ = 1/(k + h∨) diverges at the critical level, so the quantum deformation disappears and the correspondence becomes a statement about D‑modules on BunG with a central character given by an oper. Beilinson and Drinfeld showed that the category of D‑modules on BunG with a fixed central character χ : Zcrit → ℂ is equivalent to the category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the fiber of the oper map over χ.

Quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction

The construction of the Feigin–Frenkel center uses the quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction, which produces a vertex algebra Wk(𝔤) from the affine vertex algebra Vk(𝔤). At the critical level W−h∨(𝔤) is commutative and its spectrum is the space of opers. The reduction also yields the quantum Miura transformation, which relates the affine algebra to a free field realization. This free field description is essential for the explicit computation of the quantum Hitchin Hamiltonians and for the proof of the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn by Frenkel–Gaitsgory–Kazhdan–Vilonen.

Gaitsgory–Lurie Proof of the Categorical Equivalence for GLn

In a series of papers culminating in 2020, Gaitsgory and Lurie established the categorical geometric Langlands conjecture for the group GLn over a smooth projective curve X over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Their proof constructs an explicit equivalence of symmetric monoidal ∞‑categories between the derived category of D‑modules on BunGLn and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocGLn(X). The argument proceeds by induction on n, using the geometric Langlands correspondence for GL1 (which is the classical Fourier–Mukai transform on the Jacobian) and a categorical version of the Whittaker reduction that relates D‑modules on BunGLn to modules over the spherical Hecke category.

Whittaker reduction and the categorical trace

The Whittaker category Whit(BunGLn) is defined as the category of D‑modules on BunGLn equipped with a non‑degenerate character of the unipotent radical of a Borel subgroup. Gaitsgory–Lurie prove that the Whittaker reduction functor is fully faithful and its essential image is the category of modules over the spherical Hecke category, which by geometric Satake is equivalent to Rep(GLn). The categorical trace of the Hecke action then yields the desired equivalence. The proof also uses the theory of ind‑coherent sheaves on derived stacks to handle the non‑smoothness of BunGLn and LocGLn(X).

Consequences for the quantum correspondence

The categorical equivalence at the classical level implies the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn after twisting by a parameter k. The quantum deformation is realized by replacing D‑modules with k‑twisted D‑modules, which are modules over the sheaf of differential operators twisted by the determinant line bundle raised to the power k. The Gaitsgory–Lurie equivalence is compatible with this twisting, and the resulting functor intertwines the quantum Hecke functors with the tensor product by representations of the quantum group Uq(𝔰𝔩n) at q = exp(πi/(k + n)). This provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for the physical S‑duality predictions of Kapustin–Witten.

Real Geometric Langlands and the Real Hitchin System

When the curve X is equipped with an anti‑holomorphic involution σ (a real structure), one can consider G‑bundles and local systems that are equivariant with respect to σ. The real geometric Langlands program, developed by Nadler, Yun, and others, formulates a correspondence between σ‑equivariant D‑modules on the real locus BunG(ℝ) and σ‑equivariant sheaves on the real locus LocL G(ℝ). The real Hitchin system is the fixed‑point set of the involution on the complex Hitchin moduli space MH(G). Its fibers are real forms of the complex abelian varieties, often tori or products of tori and vector spaces. Mirror symmetry for the real Hitchin system exchanges the real Langlands dual groups G(ℝ) and L G(ℝ) and relates their real Hitchin fibrations.

Real opers and the Feigin–Frenkel center

At the critical level the real Feigin–Frenkel center is the algebra of functions on the space of real opers, i.e. opers equipped with a σ‑equivariant structure. The real opers form a Lagrangian subvariety of the real character variety, and the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence for real groups predicts an equivalence between categories of twisted D‑modules on the real BunG and categories of sheaves on the real oper space. This has been verified for G = SL₂(ℝ) and G = PGL₂(ℝ) using the theory of real quantum groups and the representation theory of the Virasoro algebra at central charge c = 1 − 6/(k+2)².

Applications to topological field theory

The real geometric Langlands correspondence provides boundary conditions for the topologically twisted N = 4 SYM on a four‑manifold with boundary Σ × ℝ≥0 where Σ is a real curve. The S‑duality of the bulk theory exchanges the real gauge group G(ℝ) with its Langlands dual L G(ℝ) and maps the space of boundary conditions — which are real D‑modules — to the space of real local systems. This physical picture has guided the mathematical construction of the real categorical equivalence and suggests a real version of the Gaitsgory–Lurie theorem for split real groups.

  • Confusing the classical geometric Langlands equivalence (categories of D‑modules and sheaves) with the quantum deformation (twisted D‑modules and quantum groups).
  • Assuming the geometric Satake equivalence holds for all reductive groups without the perverse sheaf condition; it requires G(𝒪)‑equivariance and the convolution product.
  • Neglecting the role of the critical level: the Feigin–Frenkel center is only commutative at k = −h∨, and the oper description fails at generic level.
  • Treating the Gaitsgory–Lurie proof as valid for arbitrary reductive groups; it is currently established only for GLn (and by extension for groups related by functoriality).
  • Overlooking the necessity of derived categories and ∞‑categorical enhancements; the equivalence does not hold on the level of abelian categories.
  • Misidentifying the real Hitchin fibers as complex abelian varieties; they are real forms that can be non‑compact and have different topology.
  • Remember that the categorical Langlands correspondence is a tensor equivalence of symmetric monoidal ∞‑categories, not merely an equivalence of triangulated categories.

Power of a Point and Radical Axis

The power of a point with respect to a circle quantifies the product of distances from the point to the two intersection points of any line through the point that meets the circle. For a point P at distance d from the centre O of a circle of radius r, the power is d² − r². If P lies outside the circle, the power equals the square of the tangent length from P to the circle; if P lies inside, the power is negative and its absolute value equals the product of the segments of any chord through P. This invariant underlies many construction problems and provides a quick way to compare lengths without solving quadratic equations.

The radical axis of two non‑concentric circles is the locus of points having equal power with respect to both circles. It is a straight line perpendicular to the line joining the centres. When the circles intersect, the radical axis coincides with their common chord; when they are tangent, it is the common tangent at the point of contact; when they are separate, it lies between them. The three radical axes of three circles taken in pairs are concurrent at the radical centre, a fact frequently used to prove collinearity or concurrency in olympiad‑style geometry and in competitive‑exam shortcut questions.

Applications include finding the length of a common external tangent: if circles have radii r₁, r₂ and centre distance d, the tangent length t satisfies t² = d² − (r₁ − r₂)². Similarly, the length of a common internal tangent uses t² = d² − (r₁ + r₂)². The radical axis also gives a linear equation when circles are expressed in Cartesian form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0; subtracting the equations eliminates the quadratic terms, leaving the line equation of the radical axis.

Examiners often embed the power of a point in problems about intersecting chords, secants, and tangents. A typical twist: a point P lies on a line that cuts a circle at A and B; another line through P cuts the same circle at C and D. The equality PA·PB = PC·PD holds regardless of the order of points, and it remains true when one of the lines becomes a tangent (then the product becomes the square of the tangent segment). Recognising this pattern converts a seemingly algebraic problem into a single‑step geometric insight.

Menelaus and Ceva Theorems in Triangle Geometry

Menelaus’ theorem gives a necessary and sufficient condition for three points on the extended sides of a triangle to be collinear. For triangle ABC and points D on BC, E on CA, F on AB (all possibly on extensions), the points are collinear iff (BD/DC)·(CE/EA)·(AF/FB) = 1, where segment lengths are taken with sign according to a chosen orientation. Ceva’s theorem is the dual statement for concurrency: lines AD, BE, CF are concurrent iff the same product equals 1. The only difference is that Menelaus deals with a transversal cutting the three sides, while Ceva deals with cevians meeting at a single point.

Both theorems work with directed segments, which automatically handle cases where the intersection points lie outside the segment. In competitive exams, the unsigned version is often used with the understanding that the product of ratios equals 1 for Ceva and −1 for Menelaus when all points are on the sides (not extensions). A common shortcut: if a cevian is a median, its ratio is 1; if it is an angle bisector, the ratio equals the adjacent side lengths; if it is an altitude, the ratio can be expressed via trigonometric functions of the base angles.

These theorems are powerful for solving problems that ask for a missing segment length when several cevians or a transversal are given. For instance, in a triangle where two cevians and one side division are known, Ceva yields the third division instantly. Menelaus is equally useful when a line through a vertex cuts the opposite side and the extensions of the other two sides — a configuration that appears frequently in “find the ratio” questions.

A typical examiner trap is to present a diagram where the transversal appears to intersect the triangle but actually meets two sides internally and the third externally. The sign convention then flips the product to −1. Candidates who blindly apply the unsigned version lose marks. Another twist: combining Ceva and Menelaus in the same figure (e.g., a cevian and a transversal intersecting) leads to a system of two equations that can be solved for two unknown ratios.

Worked Example: Ceva–Menelaus Combination
In triangle ABC, points D, E, F lie on BC, CA, AB respectively such that AD, BE, CF are concurrent at G. A line through G meets BC at X, CA at Y, and AB at Z. Given BD:DC = 2:3, CE:EA = 4:5, and AF:FB = 3:2, find the ratio BX:XC.
By Ceva, (BD/DC)·(CE/EA)·(AF/FB) = 1 → (2/3)·(4/5)·(3/2) = 1, which holds, confirming concurrency. Apply Menelaus to triangle ABC with transversal XYZ: (BX/XC)·(CY/YA)·(AZ/ZB) = 1. Since G lies on AD, BE, CF, the ratios CY/YA and AZ/ZB equal the corresponding Ceva ratios: CY/YA = CE/EA = 4/5, AZ/ZB = AF/FB = 3/2. Substitute: (BX/XC)·(4/5)·(3/2) = 1 → (BX/XC)·(12/10) = 1 → BX/XC = 10/12 = 5/6. Hence BX:XC = 5:6.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem gives three cevians or a transversal, write the Ceva or Menelaus product immediately. Use directed segments only if the diagram shows external intersections; otherwise the unsigned product with a mental sign check (odd number of external divisions ⇒ product = −1 for Menelaus) is faster. Memorise the standard ratios for medians (1), angle bisectors (adjacent sides), and altitudes (tan of base angles) to substitute instantly.

Frustums, Composite Solids, and Volume by Dissection

A frustum is the portion of a cone or pyramid that remains after the top is cut off by a plane parallel to the base. For a conical frustum with radii R (lower) and r (upper) and height h, the volume is V = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²) and the curved surface area is CSA = π(R + r)l, where l = √((R − r)² + h²) is the slant height. The total surface area adds the areas of the two circular ends. For a pyramidal frustum with base areas A₁ and A₂ and height h, the volume formula is identical in form: V = (h/3)(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)).

Composite solids are built by joining or removing basic solids (cylinders, cones, hemispheres, prisms). The key principle is additivity of volume and surface area, except that interior faces created by joining are not counted in the total surface area. A classic example: a solid formed by a cylinder of radius r and height h capped with a hemisphere of the same radius. Its volume is πr²h + (2/3)πr³; its total surface area is 2πrh + 2πr² (the base of the hemisphere coincides with the top of the cylinder and is excluded).

Dissection methods allow volume computation without memorising every formula. Cavalieri’s principle states that if two solids have equal cross‑sectional areas at every height, they have equal volumes. This principle underlies the derivation of the sphere volume from a cylinder‑cone‑hemisphere combination and is a frequent “explain why” question. In exams, you may be asked to find the volume of a solid with a known cross‑section function A(y) by integrating ∫A(y)dy; however, competitive exams usually restrict to elementary shapes where the integral reduces to a known formula.

Typical twists: a frustum is inverted and filled with liquid; find the height of the liquid when the volume is a given fraction of the total. This requires solving a cubic in the height ratio, but the similarity of the small cone to the original cone reduces it to a simple cube‑root relation: (h₁/h)³ = V₁/V. Another twist: a solid is melted and recast into a different shape; equate volumes and solve for the unknown dimension, remembering that surface area is not conserved.

Coordinate Geometry of Conics: Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola

The general second‑degree equation Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 represents a conic section. The discriminant Δ = B² − 4AC classifies it: Δ < 0 → ellipse (or circle if A = C and B = 0); Δ = 0 → parabola; Δ > 0 → hyperbola. For exam purposes, the standard forms with axes parallel to the coordinate axes are most common.

Parabola: y² = 4ax (opens right) or x² = 4ay (opens up). Focus (a,0) or (0,a), directrix x = −a or y = −a. Latus rectum length = 4a. Parametric point (at², 2at). Tangent at parameter t: ty = x + at². Normal: y = −tx + 2at + at³.

Ellipse: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b. Foci at (±c,0) where c² = a² − b². Eccentricity e = c/a. Latus rectum = 2b²/a. Parametric point (a cosθ, b sinθ). Tangent: (x cosθ)/a + (y sinθ)/b = 1. Director circle: x² + y² = a² + b² (locus of points from which perpendicular tangents can be drawn).

Hyperbola: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. Foci (±c,0) with c² = a² + b². Eccentricity e = c/a > 1. Asymptotes: y = ±(b/a)x. Parametric point (a secθ, b tanθ) or (a cosh t, b sinh t). Tangent: (x secθ)/a − (y tanθ)/b = 1. Rectangular hyperbola xy = c² has asymptotes along the axes and eccentricity √2.

Exam questions often ask for the locus of a point satisfying a geometric condition (e.g., sum of distances to two fixed points constant → ellipse). Recognising the condition and writing the equation in standard form is faster than deriving from the general quadratic. Another common pattern: find the equation of a tangent from an external point (x₁,y₁) to a conic. The combined equation of the pair of tangents is SS₁ = T², where S = 0 is the conic, S₁ is S evaluated at (x₁,y₁), and T = 0 is the tangent form with x₁,y₁ substituted. This algebraic shortcut avoids solving a quadratic in the slope.

Euler’s Formula and Polyhedral Combinatorics

Euler’s characteristic for convex polyhedra states V − E + F = 2, where V is vertices, E edges, F faces. This topological invariant holds for any polyhedron homeomorphic to a sphere. It provides a quick consistency check: a polyhedron with 12 pentagonal faces and 20 hexagonal faces (a truncated icosahedron, like a football) has F = 32. Each edge belongs to two faces, so 2E = 5·12 + 6·20 = 180 → E = 90. Then V = E − F + 2 = 90 − 32 + 2 = 60. The formula also yields the handshaking lemma for planar graphs: sum of vertex degrees = 2E.

Regular polyhedra (Platonic solids) satisfy pF = 2E = qV, where p is edges per face and q is faces meeting at each vertex. Combining with Euler gives 1/p + 1/q = 1/2 + 1/E. Since E > 0, only five integer solutions exist: (p,q) = (3,3) tetrahedron, (4,3) cube, (3,4) octahedron, (5,3) dodecahedron, (3,5) icosahedron. This derivation is a favourite proof‑type question.

For semi‑regular (Archimedean) solids, faces are regular polygons of two or more types, with identical vertex configurations. The same counting method applies: write equations for total face‑edge incidences and vertex‑edge incidences, then use Euler to solve for V, E, F. Example: a cuboctahedron has 8 triangles and 6 squares. Face‑edge count: 2E = 3·8 + 4·6 = 48 → E = 24. Vertex configuration is triangle‑square‑triangle‑square (3.4.3.4), so each vertex has degree 4: 4V = 2E = 48 → V = 12. Check: V − E + F = 12 − 24 + 14 = 2.

Examiners may ask for the number of diagonals of a polyhedron (segments joining non‑adjacent vertices). Total vertex pairs = C(V,2). Subtract edges E and face diagonals (sum over faces of C(n,2) − n for an n‑gon face). The remainder are space diagonals. For a cube (V=8, E=12, six square faces): face diagonals = 6·(C(4,2)−4) = 6·2 = 12. Total pairs = 28. Space diagonals = 28 − 12 − 12 = 4, matching the four body diagonals.

  • Assuming the radical axis always passes through the intersection points of the circles — it coincides with the common chord only when the circles intersect; otherwise it lies elsewhere.
  • Applying Menelaus with unsigned ratios when the transversal cuts one side externally — the product must be −1, not +1.
  • Forgetting to subtract the area of the common base when computing total surface area of composite solids (e.g., cylinder + hemisphere).
  • Confusing the discriminant sign for conic classification: Δ < 0 → ellipse, Δ = 0 → parabola, Δ > 0 → hyperbola.
  • Using Euler’s formula V − E + F = 2 for non‑convex or toroidal polyhedra without adjusting the characteristic (torus has V − E + F = 0).
  • Treating the latus rectum of an ellipse as 2a instead of 2b²/a, or of a hyperbola as 2a instead of 2b²/a.
  • Assuming volume is conserved but surface area is also conserved when a solid is melted and recast — only volume remains constant.

hand/cobordism-theory.html:
Unoriented and Oriented Cobordism Rings

Thom’s 1954 thesis completely determined the unoriented cobordism ring Ω*O. As a graded ℤ/2-algebra it is a polynomial ring on one generator in each dimension i that is not of the form 2k−1. The generator in dimension i can be taken to be the real projective space ℝℙi. Consequently Ω*O ≅ ℤ/2[ℝℙ1, ℝℙ2, ℝℙ4, ℝℙ5, ℝℙ6, ℝℙ8, …]. The cobordism class of a closed manifold M is detected by its Stiefel‑Whitney numbers ⟨wi1⋯wik, [M]⟩; two manifolds are cobordant iff all these numbers agree. This gives a practical algorithm: compute the total Stiefel‑Whitney class of M, expand the relevant monomials, and evaluate on the fundamental class.

The oriented cobordism ring Ω*SO is more subtle. Rationally it is a polynomial algebra on the even‑dimensional complex projective spaces: Ω*SO ⊗ ℚ ≅ ℚ[ℂℙ2, ℂℙ4, ℂℙ6, …]. The Hirzebruch signature theorem shows that the Pontryagin numbers ⟨pi1⋯pik, [M]⟩ determine the rational cobordism class. Integrally, Ω*SO contains 2‑torsion detected by Stiefel‑Whitney numbers of the underlying unoriented manifold. The structure was elucidated by Wall (1960) and Novikov: after inverting 2 the ring is polynomial on the ℂℙ2k, while the 2‑primary part is a polynomial algebra on certain Dold manifolds and Milnor’s hypersurfaces. The oriented cobordism groups in low dimensions are Ω0SO=ℤ, Ω1SO=Ω2SO=Ω3SO=0, Ω4SO=ℤ (generated by ℂℙ2), Ω5SO=ℤ/2, Ω6SO=0, Ω7SO=0, Ω8SO=ℤ⊕ℤ (generated by ℂℙ4 and ℂℙ2×ℂℙ2).

A key comparison: the forgetful map Ω*SO → Ω*O is surjective in each dimension, and its kernel is precisely the ideal generated by the classes of manifolds that bound oriented manifolds. This reflects the fact that every unoriented cobordism class contains an oriented representative after possibly taking a product with a circle. The Thom spectra MO and MSO represent these theories: MO ≃ ∨ Σi Hℤ/2 (a wedge of Eilenberg‑MacLane spectra) while MSO is more complicated, with homotopy groups π*(MSO) = Ω*SO. The Anderson‑Brown‑Peterson splitting of MSO at the prime 2 expresses it as a wedge of suspensions of MO and bo (the connective real K‑theory spectrum), making the 2‑torsion accessible to computation.

Spin and String Cobordism

A spin structure on a manifold is a lift of the structure group of the tangent bundle from SO to its double cover Spin. The spin cobordism groups Ω*Spin were computed by Anderson, Brown and Peterson (1966). After inverting 2 the ring is polynomial on generators in dimensions 4, 8, 12, … — the same as Ω*SO[1/2] — but the 2‑primary part is richer. Low‑dimensional groups are Ω0Spin=ℤ, Ω1Spin=ℤ/2, Ω2Spin=ℤ/2, Ω3Spin=0, Ω4Spin=ℤ (generated by the K3 surface), Ω5Spin=0, Ω6Spin=0, Ω7Spin=0, Ω8Spin=ℤ⊕ℤ (generated by the K3 surface squared and a certain Bott manifold). The Atiyah‑Bott‑Shapiro orientation MSpin → KO connects spin cobordism to real K‑theory; the induced map on homotopy groups sends a spin manifold to the index of its Dirac operator, which is the Â‑genus. The Â‑genus vanishes on manifolds admitting positive scalar curvature (Lichnerowicz), giving a powerful obstruction.

String structures go one step further: a string structure is a lift of the structure group from Spin to the 3‑connected cover String, which kills the first fractional Pontryagin class p1/2. The string cobordism ring Ω*String maps to the ring of integral modular forms via the Witten genus. The Ando‑Hopkins‑Rezk orientation MString → TMF (topological modular forms) lifts this genus to a map of ring spectra. The coefficient ring π*(TMF) is the ring of integral modular forms, and the Hurewicz image of the sphere in TMF is controlled by the Hopkins‑Mahowald theorem. String cobordism is therefore the natural home for elliptic cohomology and for the Stolz‑Teichner program linking supersymmetric field theories to cohomology theories.

Technique: Computing Cobordism Invariants via Characteristic Numbers
Show that the unoriented cobordism class of a closed 4-manifold is determined by its Stiefel-Whitney numbers w14, w12 w2, w22, w4. Compute these numbers for ℝℙ4 and deduce its cobordism class.
The unoriented cobordism ring Ω_*^O is a polynomial algebra over ℤ/2 on generators in dimensions not of the form 2^k-1. In dimension 4 the only generator is the class of ℝℙ4 (since 4 ≠ 2^k-1). The Stiefel-Whitney numbers of ℝℙ4 are w14 = 1, w12 w2 = 1, w22 = 0, w4 = 1 (mod 2). These numbers are not all zero, so ℝℙ4 is not null-cobordant. Because the four numbers form a basis for the ℤ/2-vector space of cobordism invariants in dimension 4, the non-vanishing of any one of them detects the generator. Hence ℝℙ4 represents the non-zero element of Ω4^O ≅ ℤ/2.
Exam strategy
When a question asks for the cobordism class of a projective space, first recall the dimension parity: ℝℙ2k is a generator in unoriented cobordism, while ℂℙ2k generates oriented cobordism after inverting 2. Write down the relevant characteristic numbers (Stiefel-Whitney for O, Pontryagin for SO) and evaluate them using the known total classes. This avoids memorising entire ring structures.

The Adams-Novikov Spectral Sequence and Chromatic Homotopy

The Adams‑Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) is the primary computational tool for stable homotopy groups of spheres using complex cobordism. Its E2-page is ExtMU*MUs(MU*, MU*(X)) and it converges to the stable homotopy groups πt−s(X) completed at a prime. For X = S0 the E2-term is Ext over the Hopf algebroid (MU*, MU*MU), which classifies formal group laws. Quillen’s theorem identifies MU* with the Lazard ring, so the ANSS is fundamentally a spectral sequence in the category of comodules over the moduli stack of formal groups Mfg.

Chromatic homotopy theory organizes the ANSS by the height of the formal group law. At a fixed prime p, the Morava K‑theories K(n) (n ≥ 1) have coefficient rings K(n)* = 𝔽p[vn±1] with |vn| = 2(pn−1). They detect height‑n phenomena. The Morava E‑theories En are Lubin‑Tate deformations of the height‑n formal group; their homotopy groups are the completed group rings of the Morava stabilizer groups. The chromatic filtration of the stable homotopy category is the tower of Bousfield localizations LK(n) → LK(n−1) → … → LK(1) → LK(0) = ℚ-localization. The telescope conjecture (still open for n ≥ 2) predicts that the finite localization with respect to a type‑n complex equals LK(n).

The ANSS E2-term for the sphere can be computed using the cobar complex on the Hopf algebroid (BP*, BP*BP) where BP is the Brown‑Peterson spectrum at a prime p. The resulting Ext groups are the cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group. For n = 1 this recovers the classical Adams spectral sequence based on mod‑p cohomology (K(1) = KU/p). For n = 2 the work of Ravenel, Shimomura, and others gave the first extensive calculations of π*(S) up to dimension ~200. The chromatic perspective explains why the stable homotopy groups of spheres are so complicated: they are built from layers of increasing height, each governed by the representation theory of a profinite group (the Morava stabilizer group). The nilpotence and periodicity theorems of Devinatz‑Hopkins‑Smith show that every element of positive degree in π*(S) is nilpotent after suitable localization, and that the telescope of a vn-self map on a type‑n complex is a K(n)-local sphere.

Cobordism Categories and the Cobordism Hypothesis

The cobordism hypothesis, conjectured by Baez and Dolan (1995) and proved by Lurie (2009), classifies fully extended topological quantum field theories (TQFTs). Let Bordn be the symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category whose objects are closed (n−1)-manifolds, 1-morphisms are n-dimensional cobordisms, 2-morphisms are cobordisms between cobordisms, and so on up to n-morphisms which are diffeomorphism classes. The hypothesis states that Bordn is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object. Consequently, giving a fully extended TQFT Z: Bordn → C (where C is any symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals) is equivalent to choosing a fully dualizable object in C. The value of Z on a point determines the entire theory.

This result has profound implications for cobordism groups. The (∞,1)-category of cobordisms up to diffeomorphism (the “non‑extended” version) has homotopy type the Thom spectrum of the universal tangent bundle. The cobordism hypothesis with singularities (proved by Ayala‑Francis‑Tanaka) extends the classification to manifolds with stratified singularities, linking cobordism groups of manifolds with G‑structure to mapping spaces into the classifying space BG. In particular, the group of invertible TQFTs (those taking values in the Picard ∞-groupoid of C) is isomorphic to the stable homotopy groups of spheres via the Pontryagin‑Thom construction. This recovers the classical fact that framed cobordism Ω*fr ≅ π*(S) and explains why anomalies in quantum field theory are classified by cobordism groups of the relevant structure group.

Applications include the classification of symmetry‑protected topological phases in condensed matter physics, where the relevant cobordism groups are those of manifolds with a map to a classifying space of the symmetry group. The Freed‑Hopkins theorem identifies the group of deformation classes of invertible topological phases with the Anderson dual of the spin cobordism spectrum MSpin. This has led to concrete computations of classification groups for various symmetry types in low dimensions, using the Adams spectral sequence for MSpin and its variants.

Applications to Manifold Classification and Exotic Spheres

Cobordism theory provides the backbone for the classification of high‑dimensional manifolds up to diffeomorphism. The Kervaire‑Milnor exact sequence (1963) relates the group Θn of h‑cobordism classes of homotopy n‑spheres (exotic spheres) to the stable homotopy groups of spheres and the image of the J‑homomorphism: 0 → bPn+1 → Θn → Coker(Jn) → 0. Here bPn+1 is the subgroup of exotic spheres that bound parallelizable manifolds; it is cyclic of order given by Bernoulli numbers for n ≡ 3 mod 4, and trivial otherwise. The J‑homomorphism J: πn(SO) → πnS arises from the Pontryagin‑Thom construction applied to the frame bundle of a manifold. Its image is completely known (Adams, 1966) and is closely tied to the denominators of Bernoulli numbers.

The surgery exact sequence of Browder‑Novikov‑Sullivan‑Wall computes the structure set S(M) of a manifold M (the set of homotopy equivalences to M modulo h‑cobordism). The obstruction to surgery lies in the Wall groups Ln(π1(M)), which are cobordism groups of quadratic forms over the group ring. For simply connected manifolds of dimension ≥ 5, the surgery obstruction map is surjective, and the classification reduces to computing the normal invariants [M, G/O] and the surgery kernel. The G/O spectrum fits into a fiber sequence G/O → BO → BG, and its homotopy groups are the cobordism groups of manifolds with a stable normal bundle lifting. This connects the classification of manifolds directly to the cobordism rings Ω*O, Ω*SO, Ω*Spin, etc.

The Kervaire invariant problem asks in which dimensions n there exists a framed manifold with Kervaire invariant 1. This is equivalent to asking whether the element hn2 in the Adams spectral sequence survives to give a non‑zero element in π2n+1−2(S). The solution by Hill‑Hopkins‑Ravenel (2016) showed that such manifolds exist only for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (and possibly n = 7, which remains open). Their proof uses the theory of topological modular forms and the chromatic filtration, illustrating how deep cobordism invariants control the existence of exotic smooth structures on spheres.

  • Confusing the generators of Ω_*^O with those of Ω_*^SO; remember ℝℙ^i generates unoriented cobordism only when i ≠ 2^k−1, while ℂℙ2k generates oriented cobordism rationally.
  • Forgetting that the Â-genus is a spin cobordism invariant, not an oriented one; it vanishes on manifolds with positive scalar curvature, a fact that does not hold for the signature.
  • Misapplying the Adams-Novikov E2-term: it is Ext over the Hopf algebroid (MU_*, MU_*MU), not over the ring MU_* alone.
  • Assuming the chromatic filtration stops at height 1; each height n contributes a layer detected by Morava K-theory K(n), and the telescope conjecture relates finite localization to K(n)-localization.
  • Overlooking the role of dualizability in the cobordism hypothesis; a fully extended TQFT is determined by a fully dualizable object, not merely by a vector space.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the Kervaire invariant and the Arf invariant; the Kervaire invariant is a framed cobordism invariant in dimensions 2^k−2, while the Arf invariant is a quadratic form invariant in dimension 2.
  • These traps highlight the most common errors in advanced cobordism theory.

hand/math-epidemiology.html:
Age-Structured Compartmental Models

Real populations mix non‑uniformly across age groups, so the homogeneous SIR model is extended by partitioning each compartment into age classes. Let the population be divided into n age groups with sizes N₁,…,Nₙ. The force of infection for group i is λᵢ = Σⱼ βᵢⱼ Iⱼ / Nⱼ, where βᵢⱼ is the transmission rate from an infectious individual in group j to a susceptible in group i. The matrix B = (βᵢⱼ) is often written as the product of a contact matrix C = (cᵢⱼ) and a per‑contact transmission probability τ, i.e. βᵢⱼ = τ cᵢⱼ. The contact matrix is estimated from diary‑based surveys (e.g. POLYMOD) and captures the average number of daily contacts between age groups.

The resulting system of ODEs for the SIR case is dSᵢ/dt = −λᵢ Sᵢ, dIᵢ/dt = λᵢ Sᵢ − γ Iᵢ, dRᵢ/dt = γ Iᵢ. The disease‑free equilibrium is Sᵢ = Nᵢ, Iᵢ = 0. Linearising the infected subsystem gives the next‑generation matrix K with entries Kᵢⱼ = (βᵢⱼ / γ) (Sᵢ⁰ / Nⱼ) = (τ cᵢⱼ / γ). The basic reproduction number R₀ is the spectral radius ρ(K). Because K is non‑negative, the Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees a positive dominant eigenvalue. This formulation shows that R₀ depends on the leading eigenvalue of the contact matrix scaled by τ/γ, not merely on the average contact rate.

Age structure also modifies the herd‑immunity threshold. If a vaccine is administered with age‑specific coverage pᵢ, the effective next‑generation matrix becomes K̃ = diag(1−pᵢ) K. The critical vaccination profile satisfies ρ(K̃) = 1. In general, the optimal allocation of a limited vaccine supply targets age groups that contribute most to the dominant eigenvector of K, a principle used in influenza and COVID‑19 prioritisation strategies.

Next‑Generation Matrix Derivation

The next‑generation matrix (NGM) provides a systematic way to compute R₀ for any compartmental model that separates new infections from transitions among infected states. Following Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Roberts (2010), write the infected‑state vector x = (x₁,…,xₘ)ᵀ. The system is dx/dt = F(x) − V(x), where Fᵢ(x) is the rate of appearance of new infections in compartment i, and Vᵢ(x) = Vᵢ⁻(x) − Vᵢ⁺(x) is the net transfer rate out of compartment i (V⁻ for outflows, V⁺ for inflows not due to new infection). At the disease‑free equilibrium x⁰, compute the Jacobians F = [∂Fᵢ/∂xⱼ] and V = [∂Vᵢ/∂xⱼ] evaluated at x⁰. The NGM is K = F V⁻¹, and R₀ = ρ(K).

For the SEIR model with compartments E (exposed) and I (infectious), the infected vector is (E, I)ᵀ. New infections enter E at rate β S I / N, so F = [[0, β], [0, 0]] at the DFE (S = N). Transfers are V = [[σ, 0], [−σ, γ]], where σ is the progression rate from exposed to infectious and γ is the recovery rate. Inverting V gives V⁻¹ = [[1/σ, 0], [1/γ, 1/γ]]. Then K = F V⁻¹ = [[β/γ, β/γ], [0, 0]]. Its spectral radius is β/γ, the familiar R₀ for SEIR. The same procedure works for multi‑host models (e.g. vector‑borne diseases) where the infected vector includes both host and vector compartments; the resulting NGM is block‑structured and its dominant eigenvalue captures the coupled transmission cycles.

An important nuance: the NGM method assumes that the disease‑free equilibrium is stable in the absence of infection (i.e. the demographic dynamics are at equilibrium). If the population is growing or has age structure, the DFE must incorporate the stable age distribution, and the matrices F and V are built on the linearised system around that demographic equilibrium. The resulting R₀ is then the asymptotic per‑generation growth factor in a fully susceptible population with the given demographic structure.

Worked Example: Two‑Age‑Group SIR
Consider a population split into children (group 1) and adults (group 2). Contact matrix C = [[12, 4], [4, 8]] contacts per day. Transmission probability per contact τ = 0.02. Recovery rate γ = 0.2 day⁻¹. Compute R₀.
The next‑generation matrix K = (τ/γ) C = (0.02/0.2) × [[12, 4], [4, 8]] = 0.1 × [[12, 4], [4, 8]] = [[1.2, 0.4], [0.4, 0.8]]. The eigenvalues of K satisfy λ² − 2.0λ + 0.8 = 0. The dominant eigenvalue is λ = (2.0 + √(4.0 − 3.2))/2 = (2.0 + √0.8)/2 ≈ (2.0 + 0.894)/2 ≈ 1.447. Hence R₀ ≈ 1.45.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for R₀ of a structured model, first write down the infected compartments, then construct F and V matrices explicitly. Do not skip the Jacobian step; examiners often award partial credit for correct F and V even if the final eigenvalue is miscalculated. Remember that R₀ is the spectral radius of F V⁻¹, not the trace or determinant.

Final Size Relation and Its Extensions

For the homogeneous SIR model, the final epidemic size Z (the fraction of the population that ever becomes infected) satisfies the transcendental equation 1 − Z = exp(−R₀ Z). This follows from integrating dS/dt = −β S I / N and dR/dt = γ I, eliminating time, and using S(∞) = N − Z N. The equation has a unique solution in (0,1) when R₀ > 1, and Z = 0 when R₀ ≤ 1. The final size relation is a powerful tool because it links the observable attack rate directly to R₀ without requiring the full time series.

In age‑structured models, the final size becomes a system of equations. Let Zᵢ be the attack rate in group i. The final susceptible fraction in group i is Sᵢ(∞)/Nᵢ = exp(−Σⱼ Kᵢⱼ Zⱼ), where K is the next‑generation matrix. Thus Zᵢ = 1 − exp(−Σⱼ Kᵢⱼ Zⱼ). This system can be solved numerically by fixed‑point iteration. The overall attack rate is the weighted average Σᵢ (Nᵢ/N) Zᵢ. Heterogeneous mixing typically reduces the overall final size compared to a homogeneous model with the same R₀, because high‑activity groups are infected early and deplete their own susceptibles, limiting further spread.

For SEIR and models with latency, the final size relation remains unchanged provided the latency period does not affect the total number of secondary infections per case. The derivation uses the fact that the total force of infection integrated over time equals the cumulative hazard experienced by susceptibles, which depends only on the total infectiousness of each case (β/γ) and not on the distribution of the infectious period. However, if the model includes waning immunity or vital dynamics, the final size concept must be replaced by the endemic equilibrium prevalence.

Parameter Estimation and Model Calibration

Fitting compartmental models to incidence data requires linking the deterministic ODE output to a statistical observation model. The most common approach assumes that reported cases C(t) follow a negative‑binomial distribution with mean ρ ∫t−1t λ(s) S(s) ds, where ρ is the reporting probability and λ(s) is the force of infection. The likelihood is then L(θ) = ∏ₜ NB(C(t) | mean(t; θ), dispersion). Parameters θ = (β, γ, ρ, …) are estimated by maximum likelihood or Bayesian inference.

Bayesian calibration uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the posterior p(θ | data) ∝ L(θ) p(θ). Prior distributions encode existing knowledge (e.g. γ ~ Gamma(shape=5, rate=1) for a mean infectious period of 5 days). Identifiability is a major concern: β and ρ often trade off, because only the product βρ is informed by case counts. Profile likelihood plots and posterior correlation matrices diagnose this. Reparameterising in terms of R₀ = β/γ and the reporting rate ρ can improve mixing.

For time‑varying transmission, β(t) is modelled as a piecewise‑constant function or a smooth spline driven by mobility data or intervention indicators. The effective reproduction number Rₜ = β(t)/γ × S(t)/N is then a derived quantity. Sequential Monte Carlo (particle filtering) or iterated filtering (IF2) are used when the latent state (S, I, R) must be inferred jointly with parameters. Model comparison via WAIC or LOO‑CV helps select between competing structures (e.g. SIR vs SEIR, with or without asymptomatic compartment).

Model Validation and Sensitivity Analysis

After calibration, a model must be validated before it is used for forecasting or policy evaluation. Posterior predictive checks simulate replicate datasets from the fitted model and compare summary statistics (peak height, peak timing, total attack rate) to the observed data. Systematic discrepancies indicate structural misspecification, such as missing age structure or behavioural feedback.

Sensitivity analysis quantifies how output metrics (R₀, final size, peak prevalence) respond to parameter variations. Local sensitivity uses partial derivatives ∂y/∂θᵢ evaluated at the posterior mean. Global sensitivity employs variance‑based methods: Sobol indices decompose the output variance into contributions from each parameter and their interactions. For high‑dimensional models, the Morris elementary effects method provides a computationally cheaper screening. Parameters with high total‑order Sobol indices are priority targets for data collection.

Structural sensitivity examines the impact of model assumptions, e.g. comparing exponential vs gamma‑distributed infectious periods (which changes the generation‑interval distribution). This is done by fitting alternative model structures to the same data and comparing their predictive performance. Ensemble forecasting, which averages predictions across a set of plausible structures weighted by their posterior model probabilities, often yields more robust projections than any single model.

  • Confusing the next‑generation matrix with the Jacobian of the full system; the NGM only involves infected compartments.
  • Assuming the final size equation 1−Z = e−R₀Z holds for any heterogeneous model without modification.
  • Treating the reporting probability ρ as known when it is usually confounded with transmission rate β.
  • Using the basic reproduction number R₀ as a direct measure of control effort without accounting for the effective reproduction number Rₜ under interventions.
  • Neglecting to check identifiability before running MCMC, leading to poorly mixed chains and misleading credible intervals.
  • Applying local sensitivity derivatives to highly non‑linear models where global interactions dominate.
  • Overlooking the effect of the generation‑interval distribution on the relationship between R₀ and the exponential growth rate r.

These advanced topics complete the core toolkit for analysing infectious disease dynamics at a level expected in competitive examinations.

Heegaard Floer Homology for Four-Manifolds and the Adjunction Inequality

Ozsváth and Szabó extended Heegaard Floer theory to smooth, closed, oriented four‑manifolds by associating to a four‑manifold X with a chosen Spinc structure a map between the Heegaard Floer groups of its boundary three‑manifolds. When X has boundary Y, the invariant takes the form of a homomorphism FX,𝔰 : HF−(Y,𝔰|Y) → HF−(∅) ≅ ℤ[U]. For a closed four‑manifold the invariant is a numerical value obtained by evaluating the map on the contact invariant of a suitable filling. The construction uses a Heegaard triple diagram (Σ,α,β,γ,w) representing a cobordism and counts holomorphic triangles in Symg(Σ). The resulting maps satisfy a composition law corresponding to gluing of cobordisms, making Heegaard Floer homology a (1+1)‑dimensional topological quantum field theory.

A central application is the adjunction inequality for smoothly embedded surfaces in symplectic four‑manifolds. Let (X,ω) be a closed symplectic four‑manifold with b2+ ≥ 2 and let Σ ⊂ X be a smoothly embedded, connected, oriented surface of genus g representing a homology class A with A·A ≥ 0. Ozsváth and Szabó proved that the Seiberg–Witten basic classes of X give a bound 2g−2 ≥ |⟨c1(𝔰),A⟩| + A·A for any Spinc structure 𝔰 with non‑zero Seiberg–Witten invariant. In Heegaard Floer language the same inequality follows from the non‑vanishing of the contact invariant c(ξ) ∈ HF−(−Y) for the contact boundary of a tubular neighbourhood of Σ. The proof uses the surgery exact triangle together with the fact that the contact invariant of the standard tight contact structure on S3 is non‑zero. This yields a purely Floer‑theoretic proof of the adjunction inequality, independent of gauge theory, and shows that Heegaard Floer homology detects the minimal genus of embedded surfaces representing a given homology class.

The four‑manifold invariants also give rise to the Ozsváth–Szabó τ invariant for knots in S3 via the large surgery formula. For a knot K, the map induced by the two‑handle attachment along K with framing n produces a chain homotopy equivalence between the mapping cone of the knot Floer complex and HF−(S3n(K)). Analysing the U‑action on this mapping cone yields the correction term d(S3n(K),𝔰) and the concordance invariant τ(K). The adjunction inequality for four‑manifolds with boundary then translates into the inequality τ(K) ≤ g4(K), where g4(K) is the smooth slice genus. This chain of arguments demonstrates how the four‑dimensional extension of Heegaard Floer homology simultaneously recovers classical gauge‑theoretic results and produces new knot concordance invariants.

Bordered Heegaard Floer Homology and the Pairing Theorem

Bordered Heegaard Floer homology, developed by Lipshitz, Ozsváth, and Thurston, assigns to a three‑manifold with parametrised boundary a differential graded module over an algebra associated to the boundary surface. For a genus g surface F with a fixed set of 2g basepoints, the algebra A(F) is a finite‑dimensional differential graded algebra generated by Reeb chords on a pointed matched circle. A bordered Heegaard diagram (Σ,α,β,z) with a single boundary component produces a left A(F)‑module CFA−(Y) and a right A(F)‑module CFD−(Y). These modules are well defined up to homotopy equivalence and satisfy a pairing theorem: if Y = Y1 ∪F Y2 is a decomposition along a surface F, then the Heegaard Floer complex of the closed manifold is homotopy equivalent to the derived tensor product CFA−(Y1) ⊗LA(F) CFD−(Y2). The proof constructs a Heegaard diagram for Y by gluing the bordered diagrams along the boundary and shows that the holomorphic curve counts in the symmetric product of the glued surface correspond exactly to the algebraic tensor product of the bordered modules.

The pairing theorem reduces the computation of HF for complicated three‑manifolds to algebraic operations on relatively small bordered modules. For example, the bordered invariant of a solid torus is a rank‑one module that encodes the framing; gluing two solid tori via a mapping class yields the Heegaard Floer homology of the resulting lens space. More generally, any three‑manifold can be built from elementary pieces (handlebodies, thickened surfaces, and mapping cylinders) whose bordered invariants are known explicitly. The algorithmic nature of the construction has led to computer implementations that compute HF for all three‑manifolds up to a given complexity. The theory also provides a natural framework for the surgery exact triangle: a Dehn surgery corresponds to replacing one bordered piece by another, and the exact triangle arises from a short exact sequence of bordered modules.

Bordered Floer homology has been extended to the “type‑D” and “type‑A” structures for manifolds with multiple boundary components, and to the “bimodule” associated to a cobordism between two surfaces. These extensions give a full 3‑2‑1 extended topological quantum field theory: a closed 3‑manifold yields a vector space, a 3‑manifold with boundary yields a module, a cobordism between surfaces yields a bimodule, and a 4‑manifold with corners yields a map between bimodules. The algebraic formalism of A∞‑modules and the derived tensor product makes the gluing theorems transparent and provides a powerful tool for proving structural results such as the invariance of the contact invariant under Legendrian surgery and the behaviour of the d‑invariant under connected sum.

Worked Example: Pairing Two Bordered Solid Tori
Let Y be the lens space L(p,q) obtained by gluing two solid tori V1 and V2 along their boundaries via the mapping class represented by the matrix ( q r ; p s ) in SL(2,ℤ). The bordered invariant CFA−(V1) is a rank‑one left A(T2)‑module generated by x with differential ∂x = 0. The right module CFD−(V2) is generated by y with differential ∂y = ρ1 y + ρ2 y, where ρ1, ρ2 are the two Reeb chord generators of A(T2). Compute the derived tensor product and identify the resulting Heegaard Floer homology groups.
The derived tensor product CFA−(V1) ⊗L CFD−(V2) is generated by x ⊗ y. The differential on the tensor product is induced by the differential on CFD− together with the left action of A(T2) on CFA−. Since ∂x = 0, the only contributions come from ∂y = ρ1 y + ρ2 y. The left module structure on CFA− is given by the action of the mapping class: ρ1·x = q x, ρ2·x = p x (up to units). Therefore ∂(x ⊗ y) = (q + p) x ⊗ y. Over ℤ/2 coefficients the differential vanishes exactly when p+q is even; otherwise the complex is acyclic. The homology is thus ℤ/2 in a single grading when p+q is even, and zero otherwise. This matches the known result that ̂HF(L(p,q)) ≅ ℤ/2p as a ℤ/2‑vector space, and the pairing theorem reproduces the correct rank after taking into account the grading shifts coming from the framing. The full ℤ‑graded calculation requires keeping track of the Maslov grading on the generators, which yields the standard absolute grading formula for lens spaces.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the effect of a Dehn surgery on Heegaard Floer homology, first identify the bordered pieces before and after surgery. Write down the corresponding type‑A and type‑D modules (they are often standard solid‑torus modules). Then apply the pairing theorem: the surgery exact triangle is the long exact sequence in homology associated to a short exact sequence of bordered modules. This algebraic viewpoint avoids re‑deriving holomorphic triangle counts and is the method expected in advanced problem sets.

The Ozsváth–Szabó Spectral Sequence from Khovanov Homology

Ozsváth and Szabó constructed a spectral sequence whose E2 page is the reduced Khovanov homology of a link L ⊂ S3 (with coefficients in ℤ/2) and which converges to the Heegaard Floer homology of the double cover Σ(L) branched along L. The construction begins with a cube of resolutions of a link diagram. Each vertex of the cube corresponds to a complete resolution, which is a collection of circles in the plane. To each resolution one associates a Heegaard diagram for the branched double cover of the corresponding tangle; the edges of the cube give rise to chain maps induced by elementary cobordisms (merge and split of circles). The total complex of this cube is a filtered chain complex whose associated graded pieces are precisely the Khovanov chain groups. The differential on the total complex counts holomorphic polygons in symmetric products of the Heegaard surfaces, and the filtration is given by the number of split circles. The spectral sequence of this filtered complex has E1 equal to the Khovanov complex and E2 equal to Khovanov homology.

The convergence of the spectral sequence to ̂HF(Σ(L)) is proved by showing that the total complex is chain homotopy equivalent to the Heegaard Floer chain complex of a Heegaard diagram for Σ(L) obtained by a branched covering construction. The key technical input is a “stretch‑the‑neck” argument that identifies the holomorphic polygons contributing to the higher differentials with the Khovanov differential and its higher analogues. As a consequence, the rank of ̂HF(Σ(L)) is bounded above by the total rank of Khovanov homology, and the spectral sequence collapses at E2 for alternating links, giving an isomorphism ̂HF(Σ(L)) ≅ Kh(L) ⊗ ℤ/2. This provides a conceptual explanation for the observed equality of ranks for alternating knots and yields a powerful computational tool: one can compute ̂HF of many branched double covers by first computing Khovanov homology (which is combinatorial) and then running the spectral sequence.

The spectral sequence also interacts with the contact invariant. The contact structure on Σ(L) induced by the standard tight contact structure on S3 corresponds under the spectral sequence to a distinguished class in Khovanov homology, often identified with the “Lee” class. This connection has been used to prove that the contact invariant of the branched double cover of a quasi‑alternating link is non‑zero, and to give a Khovanov‑homological proof of the fact that quasi‑alternating links are L‑space links. Moreover, the spectral sequence is functorial with respect to link cobordisms, leading to a map on Khovanov homology that corresponds to the four‑manifold map on Heegaard Floer homology of the branched covers. This functoriality is a key ingredient in the proof that Khovanov homology categorifies the Jones polynomial in a way compatible with the TQFT structure of Heegaard Floer homology.

Large Surgery Formula, Correction Terms, and the d‑Invariant

For a knot K ⊂ S3 and an integer framing n ≫ 0, Ozsváth and Szabó proved a large surgery formula expressing the Heegaard Floer homology of the surgered manifold S3n(K) in terms of the knot Floer complex CFK−(K). The formula states that CF−(S3n(K)) is chain homotopy equivalent to the mapping cone of a chain map vn + hn : An → Bn, where An and Bn are certain truncated subcomplexes of CFK−(K) determined by the Alexander grading. The map vn is induced by the inclusion of subcomplexes, while hn counts holomorphic disks that cross the basepoint z exactly once. The mapping cone construction yields an explicit algorithm for computing HF− of large integer surgeries from the knot Floer complex.

The correction term d(Y,𝔰) ∈ ℚ is defined for a rational homology sphere Y equipped with a Spinc structure 𝔰 as the minimal grading of a non‑torsion element in the image of HF−(Y,𝔰) → HF+(Y,𝔰). For large surgeries the d‑invariant can be read off from the mapping cone: d(S3n(K),𝔰i) = −2 max{ A(x) | x ∈ H∗(An) maps non‑trivially } + constant depending on n and i. This formula gives a practical way to compute the d‑invariants of all large surgeries once the knot Floer homology is known. In particular, for the (p,q) torus knot Tp,q the knot Floer complex is a staircase complex, and the large surgery formula reproduces the known Dedekind‑sum expression for the d‑invariants of the resulting lens spaces.

The d‑invariant satisfies a surgery exact triangle relating d(Y), d(Y0(K)), and d(Y1(K)). Combined with the large surgery formula this yields constraints on the knot Floer homology of knots with L‑space surgeries. A knot K is called an L‑space knot if some positive surgery yields an L‑space. For such knots the knot Floer homology is completely determined by the Alexander polynomial: it is a “staircase” complex with ranks given by the coefficients of ΔK(t). The large surgery formula then implies that the d‑invariants of all sufficiently large surgeries are given by a simple quadratic function of the Spinc index. This characterisation has been used to classify L‑space knots up to nine crossings and to prove that the only L‑space knots with Alexander polynomial 1 are the unknot.

Involutive Heegaard Floer Homology and the Conjugation Action

Involutive Heegaard Floer homology, introduced by Hendricks and Manolescu, refines the ordinary Heegaard Floer groups by incorporating the action of the conjugation involution on the Heegaard diagram. Given a Heegaard diagram (Σ,α,β,w) for a three‑manifold Y, the map that sends a symmetric product point {x1,…,xg} to its complex conjugate (with respect to a fixed anti‑holomorphic involution on Σ) induces a chain map ι : CF−(Y) → CF−(Y) satisfying ι2 ≃ Id. The mapping cone of 1+ι yields the involutive complex CFI−(Y), whose homology HI−(Y) carries a module structure over the ring ℤ[U,Q]/(Q2) where Q has degree −1 and UQ = QU. The ordinary Heegaard Floer homology is recovered by setting Q = 0.

The involutive correction term dI(Y,𝔰) is defined analogously to the ordinary d‑invariant but using the involutive complex. Hendricks and Manolescu proved that for any rational homology sphere Y, the inequality d(Y,𝔰) ≤ dI(Y,𝔰) ≤ d(Y,𝔰) + 1 holds. Moreover, the involutive invariant detects the non‑existence of certain orientation‑reversing involutions on Y. For example, if Y is the double cover of S3 branched along a knot K, the involution on Y corresponds to the covering transformation. The involutive Heegaard Floer homology of Σ(K) then contains information about the knot’s concordance class that is not visible in ordinary HF. In particular, the involutive τ‑invariant τI(K) gives a lower bound for the equivariant slice genus of K.

The construction extends to bordered manifolds: a bordered Heegaard diagram with an involution on the boundary surface yields a type‑D module over an involutive algebra, and the pairing theorem holds in the involutive setting. This allows the computation of HI for manifolds obtained by gluing, and leads to an involutive surgery exact triangle. The involutive theory also interacts with the contact invariant: the involutive contact invariant cI(ξ) ∈ HI−(−Y) vanishes for overtwisted contact structures and is non‑zero for many tight structures, providing a stronger obstruction to overtwistedness. Recent work has used involutive Heegaard Floer homology to prove that certain homology spheres do not bound smooth spin four‑manifolds with intersection form 2E8, a result inaccessible to ordinary Heegaard Floer homology.

  • Confusing the mapping cone in the large surgery formula with the mapping cone of the knot Floer differential; the former uses truncated subcomplexes An and Bn, not the full CFK−.
  • Assuming the Ozsváth–Szabó spectral sequence always collapses at E2; it collapses for alternating and quasi‑alternating links but can have higher differentials for general links.
  • Neglecting the grading shift when pairing bordered modules; the derived tensor product introduces a Maslov grading shift that must be accounted for to obtain the correct absolute grading on HF.
  • Treating the involutive Q‑action as a formal variable without remembering that Q2 = 0 and that U and Q commute; this leads to incorrect module structures.
  • Overlooking the requirement b2+ ≥ 2 in the adjunction inequality for symplectic four‑manifolds; the inequality fails for manifolds with b2+ = 1 without additional hypotheses.
  • Misidentifying the contact invariant c(ξ) with the generator of HF−(−Y) in all cases; c(ξ) is a specific homology class that can be zero even when HF− is non‑trivial.
  • Forgetting that the d‑invariant is defined only for rational homology spheres; for manifolds with b1 > 0 one must use the corrected invariant d∞ or work with the full HF+ module.

Fourier‑Jacobi Expansions and Jacobi Forms

The Fourier expansion of a Siegel modular form of degree two can be reorganized by separating the variable in the upper‑left entry of the period matrix. Writing the period matrix as Z = [[τ, z], [z, ω]] with τ, ω in the upper half‑plane and z in the complex plane, a Siegel modular form F of weight k admits a Fourier‑Jacobi expansion

F(τ, z, ω) = Σm≥0 φ_m(τ, z) e2π i m ω,

where each coefficient φ_m(τ, z) is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m for the full Jacobi group SL₂(ℤ) ⋉ ℤ². The theory of Jacobi forms, developed by Eichler and Zagier, provides a bridge between elliptic modular forms and Siegel modular forms: the space Jk,m of Jacobi forms is finite‑dimensional and carries a natural Hecke action compatible with the Hecke operators on Siegel modular forms. The Fourier coefficients of φ_m are indexed by pairs (n, r) ∈ ℤ² with 4nm − r² ≥ 0, and the Siegel Fourier coefficient A(T) for T = [[n, r/2], [r/2, m]] equals the (n, r)‑th Fourier coefficient of φ_m. This decomposition is essential for the proof of the Saito‑Kurokawa lift, because the Maass space consists precisely of those Siegel cusp forms whose Fourier‑Jacobi coefficients φ_m lie in the subspace of Jacobi forms that are lifts of elliptic cusp forms via the theta decomposition. Moreover, the Fourier‑Jacobi expansion yields a practical algorithm for computing Siegel modular forms: one first computes a basis of Jacobi forms for each index m, then assembles the Siegel form by matching the φ_m across indices. The dimension formulas for Jk,m (Eichler‑Zagier, Theorem 1.2) involve the genus of the modular curve X₀(m) and the representation theory of the Weil representation of SL₂(ℤ) on the space of theta series of index m.

Hecke Operators and Eigenforms on Sp(4,ℤ)

The Hecke algebra for the full Siegel modular group Sp(4,ℤ) is generated by the double cosets T(p) and T₁(p²) for each prime p, where T(p) corresponds to the diagonal matrix diag(p, p, 1, 1) and T₁(p²) to diag(p², p, p, 1). These operators act on the space M_k(Sp(4,ℤ)) of Siegel modular forms of weight k and preserve the subspace of cusp forms S_k(Sp(4,ℤ)). The commuting family {T(p), T₁(p²)}_p allows simultaneous diagonalisation; a Hecke eigenform F has eigenvalues λ_F(p) for T(p) and μ_F(p) for T₁(p²). The spinor L‑function of F is defined by the Euler product

Z_F(s) = ∏_p (1 − λ_F(p) p−s + (λ_F(p)² − μ_F(p) − p2k−3) p−2s − λ_F(p) p2k−3−3s + p4k−6−4s)−1.

For a Saito‑Kurokawa lift F = Lift(f) with f ∈ S2k−2(SL₂(ℤ)), the eigenvalues satisfy λ_F(p) = a_f(p) + pk−2 + pk−1 and μ_F(p) = p2k−3 + pk−2 a_f(p) + p2k−2, where a_f(p) are the Hecke eigenvalues of f. This relation shows that the spinor L‑function of a Saito‑Kurokawa lift factors as L(f, s) ζ(s−k+1) ζ(s−k+2). The Andrianov L‑function (the standard L‑function) of a generic Siegel eigenform is expected to be the degree‑four L‑function attached to a cuspidal automorphic representation of GSp(4, 𝔸). The multiplicity‑one theorem for Sp(4,ℤ) (proved by Weissauer for holomorphic forms) guarantees that the system of Hecke eigenvalues determines the eigenform uniquely up to scaling. The Hecke operators also act on the Fourier‑Jacobi coefficients φ_m, and the compatibility of the Hecke action with the theta decomposition is a key ingredient in the proof of the paramodular conjecture for certain abelian surfaces.

Worked Example: Hecke Eigenvalues of a Saito‑Kurokawa Lift
Let f ∈ S12(SL₂(ℤ)) be the unique normalized cusp form of weight 12 (the Ramanujan Δ‑function) with Hecke eigenvalues a_f(p) = τ(p). Compute the Hecke eigenvalues λ_F(p) and μ_F(p) for the Saito‑Kurokawa lift F = Lift(f) of weight k = 7.
For k = 7 we have k−2 = 5 and k−1 = 6. The Saito‑Kurokawa formulas give λ_F(p) = a_f(p) + p⁵ + p⁶ and μ_F(p) = p¹¹ + p⁵ a_f(p) + p¹². Since a_f(p) = τ(p), the eigenvalues are λ_F(p) = τ(p) + p⁵ + p⁶ and μ_F(p) = p¹¹ + p⁵ τ(p) + p¹². For example, at p = 2, τ(2) = −24, so λ_F(2) = −24 + 32 + 64 = 72 and μ_F(2) = 2048 + 32·(−24) + 4096 = 2048 − 768 + 4096 = 5376. These values satisfy the spinor L‑function factorisation Z_F(s) = L(f, s) ζ(s−5) ζ(s−6).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the spinor L‑function of a Siegel eigenform, first identify whether the form is a Saito‑Kurokawa lift (look for weight k and an elliptic form of weight 2k−2). If it is, write the factorisation immediately; otherwise, state the generic Euler product with λ_F(p) and μ_F(p). Memorise the two Hecke eigenvalue formulas for the lift — they appear in almost every problem set on this topic.

Theta Lifts, the Weil Representation, and the Shimura Correspondence

The Weil representation ω_ψ of the metaplectic double cover Mp(2g, ℝ) on the Schwartz space 𝒮(ℝ^g) provides a canonical way to lift automorphic forms from orthogonal groups to symplectic groups. For a positive‑definite even lattice L of rank 2g, the theta series Θ_L(Z) = Σx∈L eπ i (x, x) Z is a Siegel modular form of weight g/2 for a congruence subgroup of Sp(2g, ℤ). The Siegel‑Weil formula, proved by Weil and later refined by Kudla and Rallis, expresses the integral of Θ_L against an Eisenstein series on the orthogonal group as a Siegel Eisenstein series on Sp(2g). This identity yields the analytic continuation and functional equation of the Siegel Eisenstein series and gives a precise formula for its Fourier coefficients in terms of representation numbers of quadratic forms. The Shimura correspondence is the special case g = 1: it lifts a half‑integral weight modular form f(τ) = Σ c(n) q^n (with n ≡ 0,1 mod 4) to an integral weight form F(z) = Σ (Σd|n dk−1 c(n²/d²)) q^n on SL₂(ℤ). In higher degree, the theta lift from O(2g) to Sp(2g) sends a cuspidal automorphic representation π of the orthogonal group to a cuspidal representation Θ(π) of the symplectic group, provided the local theta correspondence is non‑zero. The non‑vanishing criterion is governed by the local Langlands correspondence and the epsilon‑factor ε(½, π, std). The Ikeda lift can be interpreted as an iterated theta lift from a pair of elliptic modular forms to Sp(2n), and the Yoshida lift arises from a theta lift from a product of two modular curves to Sp(4). These constructions realise Langlands functoriality for the dual pair (O(2g), Sp(2g)) and are central to the endoscopic classification of Siegel modular forms.

The Paramodular Conjecture and Abelian Surfaces

The paramodular conjecture, formulated by Brumer and Kramer, predicts a bijection between isogeny classes of abelian surfaces A/ℚ with End(A) = ℤ and paramodular Siegel cusp forms of degree two, weight two, and level N equal to the conductor of A, with rational Hecke eigenvalues. A paramodular form is a Siegel modular form for the paramodular group K(N) = Sp(4, ℚ) ∩ M4(ℤ) with certain diagonal entries divisible by N. The conjecture extends the modularity theorem for elliptic curves (weight two, level N, trivial character) to dimension two. Evidence includes the work of Poor and Yuen, who computed paramodular forms for many levels and matched their L‑functions with those of abelian surfaces found by Cremona and Sutherland. The spinor L‑function of a paramodular eigenform F satisfies a functional equation relating s to 3−s, and its special value at s = 1 is conjecturally related to the order of the Tate‑Shafarevich group of A via the Bloch‑Kato conjecture. The paramodular group K(N) is not conjugate to a subgroup of Sp(4, ℤ) for N > 1, so the theory of Hecke operators for paramodular forms requires the double coset algebra of the adelic group GSp(4, 𝔸_f) with respect to the compact open subgroup K(N)̂. The local Hecke algebra at a prime p ∤ N is generated by the same operators T(p) and T₁(p²) as for the full level, but at p | N the operators are modified and the eigenvalues encode the reduction type of A at p. The conjecture also predicts that the paramodular form is a Gritsenko lift (a lift from Jacobi forms) exactly when the abelian surface has a non‑trivial endomorphism algebra over a quadratic field, linking the paramodular conjecture to the theory of Jacobi forms and the Maass space.

The Gan‑Gross‑Prasad Conjecture for Symplectic Groups and Period Integrals

The Gan‑Gross‑Prasad (GGP) conjecture for the pair (GSpin(5), GSpin(4)) ≅ (GSp(4), GL(2) × GL(2)) predicts a precise relation between the non‑vanishing of a period integral of a cuspidal automorphic form on GSp(4) over the diagonal subgroup GL(2) and the central value of the Rankin‑Selberg L‑function L(½, π × τ), where π is the automorphic representation of GSp(4) and τ is the representation of GL(2) × GL(2) obtained by restriction. In the classical language, let F be a Siegel cusp form of degree two and weight k, and let f, g be elliptic cusp forms of weights k₁, k₂. The period integral ∫Γ\ℍ² F(Z) f(τ₁) g(τ₂) (det Y)k−3 dX dY (with Z = X + iY, τ₁, τ₂ the diagonal entries) is expected to be non‑zero if and only if L(½, F × f × g) ≠ 0. The conjecture has been proved in many cases by Ichino‑Ikeda (for unitary groups) and by Xue (for symplectic groups) using the relative trace formula. The GGP conjecture for GSp(4) implies a formula for the central derivative of the spinor L‑function when the central value vanishes, which is a key input for the Bloch‑Kato conjecture for the motive attached to F. Moreover, the GGP period appears in the Gross‑Zagier formula for Heegner cycles on the Siegel modular threefold, linking heights of cycles to derivatives of L‑functions. The conjecture also governs the non‑vanishing of the Yoshida lift: the Yoshida lift of a pair (f, g) is non‑zero precisely when the period of the corresponding Siegel form over the diagonal GL(2) is non‑zero, which by GGP is equivalent to L(½, f × g) ≠ 0. This provides a conceptual explanation for the classical criterion of Yoshida and connects the theory of Siegel modular forms to the broader framework of the Langlands program.

  • Confusing the Maass space with the full space of Siegel cusp forms — the Maass space is a proper subspace characterised by Fourier coefficients depending only on the GL₂(ℤ)‑orbit of the matrix T.
  • Assuming the Saito‑Kurokawa lift is surjective onto the Maass space for all weights — it is an isomorphism only for even weight k ≥ 3; for odd weight the Maass space is zero.
  • Misapplying the Hecke eigenvalue formulas for the lift to generic Siegel eigenforms — the formulas λ_F(p) = a_f(p) + pk−2 + pk−1 and μ_F(p) = p2k−3 + pk−2 a_f(p) + p2k−2 hold only for Saito‑Kurokawa lifts.
  • Overlooking the level‑dependence in the paramodular conjecture — the paramodular group K(N) changes with the conductor N, and Hecke operators at primes dividing N are not the standard T(p), T₁(p²).
  • Treating the Gan‑Gross‑Prasad period as always non‑zero — the conjecture precisely characterises when it vanishes in terms of the central L‑value, and many explicit examples have zero period.
  • Neglecting the role of the Weil representation in the Siegel‑Weil formula — the formula equates an integral of a theta series (built from the Weil representation) with a Siegel Eisenstein series, and this identity is the source of the functional equation.
  • Confusing the Ikeda lift with the Saito‑Kurokawa lift — the Ikeda lift produces forms on Sp(2n) for any n ≥ 2, while the Saito‑Kurokawa lift is the special case n = 2 with weight shifted by one.

These advanced topics complete the core knowledge required for research‑level work on Siegel modular forms.
